 In North Carolina, a legal battle is ongoing regarding the prohibition of ballot selfies, which has its roots in the state's efforts to combat voter fraud. The controversy began in 2024 when a Libertarian voter took a selfie in a ballot box, claiming her First Amendment rights allowed her to do so. The State Board of Elections argues that allowing such selfies could facilitate vote-buying schemes by providing a form of proof that individuals voted a specific way. Critics of the ban point out that there is no substantial evidence of vote-buying schemes occurring based on ballot selfies and assert that citizens should have the right to advocate for their political choices freely. The judicial conversation surrounding this issue highlights the state's emphasis on election secrecy, allowing other forms of political expression while maintaining the ban on ballot selfies. Historical context reveals that concerns about coercion and bribery in voting date back to the 1800s, leading to the development of secret ballots. While North Carolina has joined at least 14 other states in banning ballot selfies, some states like New Hampshire have successfully challenged such prohibitions in the courts, arguing that the focus should be on prosecuting bribery instead of restricting free speech. (© WRAL) 
 By Will Doran, WRAL state government reporter
 More than one-third of North Carolina’s eligible voters have already cast a ballot in this year’s midterm elections. If weren't one of them, Tuesday is your last chance to vote. And you’ll likely have to do it in person. 
 Polls across the state will be open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. Tuesday. And unlike during early voting, voters are assigned specific precincts for voting on Election Day.
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 Voters in North Carolina appear enthusiastic this year, setting a new record for voter turnout during early voting in a midterm. New numbers published Sunday by state officials show that  more than 2.8 million people had voted  during early voting, which ended the day prior, or by mail so far. That represents nearly 36% of the state's registered voters.
 And Democrats have a turnout advantage as of the end of early voting on Saturday. While Republicans and Democrats each make up 29% of the state's total voters, just 26% of ballots cast during early voting or by mail so far have been from Republicans, while 38% have come from Democrats.
 To find your precinct to vote Tuesday — or to confirm that it hasn’t changed since the last time you voted — you can look up your voter registration information online.
 Using the state’s voter search tool , people can find both their polling place location and their sample ballot, showing all the races they’ll have a chance to vote on this year.
 What’s on the ballot
 Congress and state legislature: The U.S. Senate contest is the premier race on the ballot this year and will be chosen by voters from all across North Carolina. Everyone will also be voting on their representatives in the U.S. House of Representatives , and all 170 seats in the state General Assembly . Those seats are elected by districts, instead of statewide, so you’ll only vote in the districts where your home is located.
 Constitutional amendments: Every voter in the state can also vote on whether to approve three proposed amendments to the North Carolina Constitution: One to restrict the ability of local governments to raise property taxes , one to permanently ban income taxes from rising above 3.5% in the future, and one to enshrine the state’s voter photo-identification laws.
 Judges and local races: Four appellate judicial seats — three on the state Court of Appeals and one seat on the state Supreme Court — will be decided by voters across the state. There are also dozens of local, county-level elections for trial court judges. And those are far from the only local elections this year. Voters in at least some areas can also select their local sheriffs, prosecutors, city and town council members, school board members — including Wake County’s District 1 , District 2 , District 7 and District 9 — and county commissioners, among other seats.
 Fundraising referendum votes: Voters in some cities or counties will also be asked to approve or deny bond referendum requests. Those allow local governments to take out loans for specific purposes, sometimes but not always at the cost of higher property taxes. Schools, parks and affordable housing initiatives are frequent bond targets. In the state’s largest county, Wake County voters will be asked to vote on two referenda — for construction and renovation of K-12 schools and community colleges — totaling more than $829 million. If approved, they’re expected to cause property taxes to increase by $5 for every $100,000 of a property’s value.
 How can I follow the results on election night?
 Find results on WRAL-TV or WRAL News+ throughout the evening. We’ll be following the top races and their broader impact, such as possible changes to the balance of power in the U.S. Congress or the North Carolina General Assembly. You can also visit WRAL.com for updates to articles on the elections, as well as real-time election results once polls close, pulled directly from data reported by the State Board of Elections. The state elections board also maintains a results page.
 Can I still vote by mail?
 Mail-in ballots will be thrown out if they arrive after Election Day, even if they were postmarked before then, due to a relatively new state law. So if you haven’t already filled out your ballot and mailed it back, it’s likely too late to do so at this point unless you want to pay for expedited shipping. And even then, there’s no guarantee it’ll be delivered in time. 
 People who requested mail-in ballots but haven’t returned them yet still have options: You can go vote in person Tuesday instead. Just because you requested a mail-in ballot doesn’t require you to vote that way. Or, you can hand-deliver your mail-in ballot to your home county’s board of elections office on Monday or Tuesday, before polls close at 7:30 p.m.
 If you’ve already mailed your ballot, you can track its progress through the mail using the state's BallotTrax app .
 What should I bring to the polls?
 A photo ID is required to vote. Accepted IDs include a North Carolina driver's license, U.S. passport and certain state-issued or approved student IDs. Most IDs must be unexpired or expired for one year or less. Different rules apply to voters 65 and older, military IDs and certain other forms of identification.
 If you forget your ID , you can still cast a provisional ballot and bring an acceptable ID to your county elections board no later than 12 p.m. on Nov. 10.
 If you don’t have ID , you can request an exemption — but only if you can claim one of multiple acceptable reasons for not having an ID. State officials recently rewrote the rules to make it easier to throw out people's ballots if election administrators decide they don't believe a voters' claim on that exemption form.
 Can I bring my phone?
 Yes, you are allowed to bring your phone to look up candidate information. But taking a photo of your completed ballot is illegal , and voters aren’t allowed to use their phones to communicate with others while inside the voting booth.
 What if I need assistance?
 Curbside voting is available for voters who aren’t able to enter a polling place without physical assistance because of age or disability. Voters may also request help from poll workers or bring an eligible person to assist them.
 What if I run into problems at the polls?
 Voter intimidation is illegal in North Carolina, and poll workers are trained on how to handle reports of politicians, activists or regular people being overly aggressive outside a polling place, or perhaps of watching others too closely inside by the voting booths. If you feel intimidated you can ask one of the precinct officials on site for help or advice. You can also contact your local county Board of Elections officials. It is also a crime to interfere with election officials.
 Many nonprofit groups, separate from the government, also have voting assistance teams that help people who run into issues with poll workers or others. One large alliance between many nonpartisan voting rights groups runs the Protect Our Vote NC Coalition. People can file reports with them by texting or calling 1-888-OUR-VOTE.
